lesson.title: The Breadbasket Between New England and the South
lesson.summary: Sitting geographically and culturally between New England and the southern colonies, the Middle Colonies of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware grew into some of England's most ethnically diverse and agriculturally productive holdings in North America.
lesson.body:
The Middle Colonies did not begin as English territory at all. Dutch traders and settlers established New Netherland in the early 1600s, founding New Amsterdam at the mouth of the Hudson River around 1624 as a fur trading post and colonial capital. The Dutch colony brought a mix of European settlers, including Dutch, Walloon, and other nationalities, and practiced a degree of religious tolerance unusual for the period, setting a pattern of diversity that would outlast Dutch rule itself. England seized the colony in 1664 during a period of Anglo Dutch rivalry and renamed it New York, after James, Duke of York, the king's brother who had been granted the territory.

Pennsylvania took shape under very different circumstances, arising from one man's religious convictions. William Penn, a Quaker who had faced persecution in England for his faith, received a massive land grant from King Charles II in 1681, reportedly in settlement of a debt the crown owed Penn's late father. Penn intended the colony as what he called a holy experiment, a place where Quakers and other persecuted religious groups could practice their faith freely, and he extended that tolerance broadly, welcoming German, Welsh, and other European settlers alongside English Quakers. Penn also pursued relatively peaceful relations with the Lenape, the indigenous people of the region, negotiating land purchases and treaties that, while later mythologized, generally avoided the large scale violence seen in some other colonies during this period.

New Jersey and Delaware developed as smaller neighboring territories carved from these larger holdings, absorbing similar patterns of mixed European settlement and, in Delaware's case, a legacy of earlier Swedish colonization along the Delaware River that predated both Dutch and English control.

What united the Middle Colonies economically was fertile land well suited to grain farming, particularly wheat, which colonists exported in large quantities, earning the region a reputation as the breadbasket of English North America. Philadelphia, Penn's carefully planned capital, grew into one of the busiest ports and largest cities in all the colonies by the eighteenth century, benefiting from this agricultural export trade as well as its position as a hub for immigrants arriving from across Europe.

This combination of ethnic and religious diversity, productive agriculture, and commercial vitality gave the Middle Colonies a distinct character, less uniformly commercial than Virginia's tobacco economy and less centered on a single religious vision than Puritan New England. Built on the same English exploration and colonization impulses that produced Jamestown and Plymouth, the Middle Colonies nonetheless became something genuinely their own, a pluralistic, agriculturally rich middle ground between England's northern and southern American holdings.
